Close to the Sun, Mercury races. Far out, Neptune crawls.
So the outer stars of a galaxy should crawl too.
In 1970, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast sixty-seven glowing gas clouds were moving in the Andromeda galaxy.
The speeds rose, then stayed high, at about two hundred seventy kilometres a second.
The outer clouds were not slowing down.
Ten years and twenty-one galaxies later, Rubin's team called the conclusion inescapable: matter that gives off no light lies beyond the visible galaxy.
Today we call it dark matter.
What is it made of? Nobody knows yet.
